summary: This paper derives analytical upper and lower bounds on the failure probability of Shor-style fault-tolerant quantum error correction (FT-QEC) schemes under depolarizing noise, explicitly accounting for faulty gates and measurements. The analysis separates two failure mechanisms: decoding errors (when the decoder fails to correct) and residual errors (undetected errors from the FT circuit itself that escape a single syndrome extraction round).
motivation: While QEC is essential for scalable quantum computation, practical implementations require fault-tolerant circuits, but most analyses assume idealized components. Understanding performance limits under realistic circuit-level faults is crucial for designing reliable quantum systems.
method: Using limited structural information (number of flag qubits, gate counts), the authors derive upper bounds on decoding failure probability $P_{\mathrm{fail,dec}}$ via probabilistic counting of error propagation paths, and both upper and lower bounds on residual error probability $P_{\mathrm{res}}$. Analysis covers flag-based and cat-state syndrome extraction for CSS codes including surface codes, rotated surface codes, and color codes, with depolarizing error model having probability $p$ for channel errors and $p_{\mathrm{FT}}$ for gate/measurement faults.
result: For the $[[13,1,3]]$ surface code with $p_{\mathrm{FT}} = p/10$, the refined bound (Theorem 1) shows $P_{\mathrm{fail,dec}}$ degrades significantly compared to ideal ($p_{\mathrm{FT}}=0$) performance; the asymptotic upper bound on $P_{\mathrm{res}}$ (Theorem 3) is tight at low error rates, and combined bounds demonstrate that residual errors impose fundamental limits even for theoretically sound codes, with simulations validating the analytical predictions.
